claim: HSCs activate the glycolytic rate-limiting enzyme phosphofructokinase (PFK) during proliferation and oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) inhibition.
source: Through quantitative 13C metabolic flux analysis of glucose metabolism using high-sensitivity glucose tracing and mathematical modeling, we found that HSCs activate the glycolytic rate-limiting enzyme phosphofructokinase (PFK) during proliferation and oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) inhibition.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from 13C metabolic flux analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Proliferative stress or OXPHOS inhibition led to accelerated glycolysis via increased activity of PFKFB3 within seconds to meet ATP requirements.
source: Real-time measurement of ATP levels in single HSCs demonstrated that proliferative stress or OXPHOS inhibition led to accelerated glycolysis via increased activity of PFKFB3, the enzyme regulating an allosteric PFK activator, within seconds to meet ATP requirements.
evidence: The claim is supported by real-time ATP measurement data using the GO-ATeam2 system.

claim: Varying stresses differentially activated PFKFB3 via PRMT1-dependent methylation during proliferative stress and via AMPK-dependent phosphorylation during OXPHOS inhibition.
source: Furthermore, varying stresses differentially activated PFKFB3 via PRMT1-dependent methylation during proliferative stress and via AMPK-dependent phosphorylation during OXPHOS inhibition.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunocytochemistry data showing PFKFB3 methylation and phosphorylation under different stress conditions.

claim: Overexpression of Pfkfb3 induced HSC proliferation and promoted differentiated cell production.
source: Overexpression of Pfkfb3 induced HSC proliferation and promoted differentiated cell production, whereas inhibition or loss of Pfkfb3 suppressed them.
evidence: The claim is supported by cell cycle analysis and transplantation experiments showing increased proliferation and differentiation with Pfkfb3 overexpression.

claim: Inhibition or loss of Pfkfb3 suppressed HSC proliferation and differentiated cell production.
source: Overexpression of Pfkfb3 induced HSC proliferation and promoted differentiated cell production, whereas inhibition or loss of Pfkfb3 suppressed them.
evidence: The claim is supported by CRISPR-Cas9 knockout experiments and inhibitor studies showing decreased proliferation and differentiation.

claim: ATP is the universal energy currency of all organisms and regulates all anabolic or catabolic cellular activities.
source: ATP, produced via cytosolic glycolysis and mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS), is the universal energy currency of all organisms; it regulates all anabolic or catabolic cellular activities (Schirmer and Evans, 1990; Denton et al., 1975; Harris et al., 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to established scientific literature.

claim: Precise control of intracellular ATP concentrations is critical, as ATP is the rate determiner of many ATP-dependent biochemical reactions.
source: Precise control of intracellular ATP concentrations is critical, as ATP is the rate determiner of many ATP-dependent biochemical reactions (Sols, 1981; Gabriel et al., 1985; Frieden, 1965; Hardie et al., 2012; Lin and Hardie, 2018; Hardie and Carling, 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to established scientific literature.

claim: HSCs possess unique cell cycle quiescence, high self-renewal and differentiation capacity in response to stimuli, and resistance to cellular stress.
source: Among the HSPC fractions, HSCs possess unique cell cycle quiescence, high self-renewal and differentiation capacity in response to stimuli, and resistance to cellular stress, including reactive oxygen species and physiological aging (Pinho and Frenette, 2019; Busch et al., 2015; Sun et al., 2014; Ho et al., 2017; Laurenti and Göttgens, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to established scientific literature.

claim: Glycolytic enzymes maintain HSCs and hematopoietic progenitor cells (HPCs) by regulating cellular survival and cell cycle quiescence.
source: Among the known regulators of ATP-producing pathways, glycolytic enzymes maintain HSCs and hematopoietic progenitor cells (HPCs) by regulating cellular survival and cell cycle quiescence (Takubo et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2014; Simsek et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Loss of mitochondrial genes in HPSCs induces HSC differentiation defects.
source: Loss of mitochondrial genes in HPSCs also induces HSC differentiation defects (Inoue et al., 2010; Yu et al., 2013; Bejarano-García et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Disrupting the mitochondrial complex III subunit depletes both differentiated hematopoietic cells and quiescent HSCs.
source: Moreover, disrupting the mitochondrial complex III subunit depletes both differentiated hematopoietic cells and quiescent HSCs (Ansó et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Pyruvate dehydrogenase kinase activity, which can uncouple glycolysis and the TCA cycle, is required to maintain HSC function.
source: Although glycolysis and the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle are metabolically linked, pyruvate dehydrogenase kinase activity, which can uncouple these pathways, is required to maintain HSC function (Takubo et al., 2013; Halvarsson et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: During HSC division, cell metabolism is reprogrammed to activate fatty acid β-oxidation (FAO) and purine metabolism.
source: During HSC division, cell metabolism is reprogrammed to activate fatty acid β-oxidation (FAO) and purine metabolism (Ito et al., 2012; Karigane et al., 2016; Umemoto et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Activated HSCs mainly rely on glycolysis as their energy source.
source: Furthermore, Liang et al. reported that activated HSCs mainly rely on glycolysis as their energy source (Liang et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous research by Liang et al.

claim: Deeply quiescent HSCs do not activate cell cycle under stress.
source: Recently, it has been shown that deeply quiescent HSCs do not activate cell cycle under stress (Bowling et al., 2020; Fanti et al., 2023; Munz et al., 2023).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to recent research.

claim: 5-FU administration induced cell cycle progression of entire HSCs in mice.
source: These results indicated that 5-FU administration induced cell cycle progression of entire HSCs in mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing increased pRb and decreased G0 marker expression in HSCs after 5-FU treatment.

claim: In 5-FU-treated HSCs, the levels of glycolytic metabolites derived from U-13C6-glucose were double those observed in PBS-treated HSCs.
source: In 5-FU-treated HSCs, the levels of glycolytic metabolites derived from U-13C6-glucose were double those observed in PBS-treated HSCs (Figure 1B–C; Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by IC-MS tracer analysis data shown in Figure 1B-C.

claim: The total levels of TCA cycle intermediates derived from U-13C6-glucose were similar between PBS- and 5-FU-treated cells.
source: The total levels of TCA cycle intermediates derived from U-13C6-glucose were similar between PBS- and 5-FU-treated cells (Figure 1D; Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by IC-MS tracer analysis data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Levels of U-13C6-glucose-derived intermediates involved in the pentose phosphate pathway (PPP) and nucleic acid synthesis (NAS) were twofold higher in 5-FU-treated than in PBS-treated HSCs.
source: Levels of U-13C6-glucose-derived intermediates involved in the pentose phosphate pathway (PPP) and nucleic acid synthesis (NAS) were twofold higher in 5-FU-treated than in PBS-treated HSCs, whereas no significant differences in the levels of metabolites were observed between both groups (Figure 1E–F; Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by IC-MS tracer analysis data shown in Figure 1E-F.

claim: Compared to PBS-treated HSCs, 5-FU-treated HSCs exhibited a higher extracellular acidification rate (ECAR), while their oxygen consumption rate (OCR) remained equal to that of PBS-treated HSCs.
source: Compared to PBS-treated HSCs, 5-FU-treated HSCs exhibited a higher extracellular acidification rate (ECAR), while their oxygen consumption rate (OCR) remained equal to that of PBS-treated HSCs (Figure 1G–H; Figure 1—figure supplement 3A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by Seahorse flux analyzer data shown in Figure 1G-H.

claim: Regardless of the EPCR expression, the 2-NBDG uptake was greater in HSCs treated with 5-FU than in those treated with PBS.
source: Regardless of the EPCR expression, the 2-NBDG uptake was greater in HSCs treated with 5-FU than in those treated with PBS (Figure 1J–L).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo 2-NBDG uptake data shown in Figure 1J-L.

claim: HSCs cultured under cytokine-rich proliferative conditions were more resistant to the inhibition of OXPHOS by oligomycin compared to HSCs cultured under quiescence-maintaining conditions.
source: Furthermore, compared to HSCs cultured under the quiescence-maintaining conditions of HSC achieved by hypoxia, abundant fatty acids, and low cytokines as we previously reported (Kobayashi et al., 2019), HSCs cultured under cytokine-rich proliferative conditions were more resistant to the inhibition of OXPHOS by oligomycin (Figure 1—figure supplement 1N; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell culture data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1N.

claim: 5-FU-treated HSCs exhibited activated glycolytic flux, increasing the turnover of ATP.
source: Overall, the results showed that 5-FU-treated HSCs exhibited activated glycolytic flux, increasing the turnover of ATP.
evidence: The claim is inferred from multiple experimental results including tracer analysis and Seahorse data.

claim: Glycolytic flux into mitochondria was equally unchanged in PBS- and 5-FU-treated-HSCs, supporting that 5-FU activated anaerobic glycolysis in HSCs.
source: Moreover, glycolytic flux into mitochondria was equally unchanged in PBS- and 5-FU-treated-HSCs, supporting that 5-FU activated anaerobic glycolysis in HSCs.
evidence: The claim is supported by TCA cycle metabolite data from tracer analysis.

claim: Oligomycin-treated HSCs exhibited glycolytic system activation.
source: Similar to 5-FU-treated HSCs (Figure 1), oligomycin-treated HSCs exhibited glycolytic system activation (Figure 2B–C; Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by IC-MS tracer analysis data shown in Figure 2B-C.

claim: Metabolite flux to the TCA cycle and PPP was unchanged, but flux to the NAS was significantly reduced in oligomycin-treated HSCs compared to that in steady-state HSCs.
source: Metabolite flux to the TCA cycle and PPP was unchanged, but flux to the NAS was significantly reduced in oligomycin-treated HSCs compared to that in steady-state HSCs (Figure 2D–F; Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by IC-MS tracer analysis data shown in Figure 2D-F.

claim: OXPHOS-inhibited HSCs activated compensatory glycolytic flux and suppressed NAS flux.
source: The results suggested that OXPHOS-inhibited HSCs activated compensatory glycolytic flux and suppressed NAS flux.
evidence: The claim is inferred from tracer analysis data showing increased glycolytic metabolites and decreased NAS metabolites.

claim: ECAR were elevated in HSCs after oligomycin treatment compared to before oligomycin treatment.
source: The results showed that ECAR were elevated in HSCs after oligomycin treatment compared to before oligomycin treatment (Figure 2G; Figure 1—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by Seahorse flux analyzer data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: No increase in ECAR was observed in MyPs after oligomycin treatment.
source: No increase in ECAR was observed in MyPs (Figure 2G; Figure 1—figure supplement 3C), supporting that inhibition of OXPHOS activated anaerobic glycolysis specifically in HSCs.
evidence: The claim is supported by Seahorse flux analyzer data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: In HSCs, the decrease in OCR after oligomycin administration was less evident compared to MyPs.
source: Meanwhile, in HSCs, the decrease in OCR after oligomycin administration was less evident compared to MyPs (Figure 2H; Figure 1—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by Seahorse flux analyzer data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: The variation in the flux values of all enzymatic reactions calculated in HSCs after 5-FU or oligomycin treatment became smaller compared to quiescent HSCs.
source: As a result, the variation in the flux values of all enzymatic reactions calculated in HSCs after 5-FU or oligomycin treatment became smaller compared to quiescent HSCs, suggesting that HSCs strictly regulated their metabolism in response to stress (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by 13C-MFA simulation data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-C.

claim: HSCs treated with 5-FU or oligomycin exhibited preferential glycolytic activation rather than TCA- or PPP-based metabolic strategies.
source: Unlike PBS-treated HSCs, those treated with 5-FU or oligomycin exhibited preferential glycolytic activation rather than TCA- or PPP-based metabolic strategies; the first half of the glycolytic system appeared to be the site of metabolic activation (Figure 3A–J; Figure 3—figure supplement 1D–U, Supplementary file 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by 13C-MFA data shown in Figure 3A-J.

claim: The ratio of fructose 1,6-bisphosphate (F1,6BP) to F6P was greatly elevated in HSCs during proliferation and OXPHOS inhibition.
source: A detailed review of in vitro isotope tracer analysis results showed that the ratio of fructose 1,6-bisphosphate (F1,6BP; the product of PFK) to F6P (the substrate of PFK) was greatly elevated in HSCs during proliferation and OXPHOS inhibition (Figure 3K–L).
evidence: The claim is supported by tracer analysis data shown in Figure 3K-L.

claim: HSCs exhibit elevated glycolytic flux relative to mitochondrial activity by increasing PFK enzyme activity under various stress conditions.
source: Together with the results of quantitative 13C-MFA, these findings suggested that HSCs exhibit elevated glycolytic flux relative to mitochondrial activity by increasing PFK enzyme activity under various stress conditions.
evidence: The claim is inferred from 13C-MFA and tracer analysis data.

claim: In HSCs from 5-FU-treated mice, we observed increased labeling of glycolytic metabolites such as dihydroxyacetone phosphate, glycerol-3-phosphate, and phosphoenolpyruvate, as well as NAS metabolites such as inosine monophosphate and ATP, and those derived from TCA cycle such as aspartic acid and glutamate, compared to HSCs from PBS-treated mice.
source: In HSCs from 5-FU-treated mice, we observed increased labeling of glycolytic metabolites such as dihydroxyacetone phosphate, glycerol-3-phosphate, and phosphoenolpyruvate, as well as NAS metabolites such as inosine monophosphate and ATP, and those derived from TCA cycle such as aspartic acid and glutamate, compared to HSCs from PBS-treated mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B–I, Supplementary file 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo tracer analysis data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B-I.

claim: More glucose-derived metabolites entered TCA cycle in the 5-FU-treated group than PBS-treated group.
source: When the amount of U-13C6-glucose-derived labeled metabolites in each pathway was calculated, more glucose-derived metabolites entered TCA cycle in the 5-FU-treated group than PBS-treated group (Figure 3—figure supplement 2J).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo tracer analysis data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2J.

claim: The number of bone marrow mononuclear cells (BMMNCs), as well as the frequency of HSCs (CD150+CD48-LSK) and other progenitor cells, in the bone marrow (BM) of GO-ATeam2+ mice were almost unchanged compared to of C57B6/J mice, except for a mild decrease in the Lin- fraction.
source: The number of bone marrow mononuclear cells (BMMNCs), as well as the frequency of HSCs (CD150+CD48-LSK) and other progenitor cells, in the bone marrow (BM) of GO-ATeam2+ mice were almost unchanged compared to of C57B6/J mice, except for a mild decrease in the Lin- fraction (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-C.

claim: MyPs showed more rapid decreases in ATP concentration than HSCs.
source: MyPs showed more rapid decreases in ATP concentration than HSCs, suggesting higher ATP consumption by progenitors (Figure 4—figure supplement 1G–H).
evidence: The claim is supported by GO-ATeam2 ATP measurement data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1G-H.

claim: Adding glucose to the medium suppressed ATP decrease in MyPs; however, other metabolites (e.g. pyruvate, lactate, and fatty acids) had minimal effects, suggesting that ATP levels are glycolysis-dependent in MyPs.
source: Adding glucose to the medium suppressed this decrease in MyPs; however, other metabolites (e.g. pyruvate, lactate, and fatty acids) had minimal effects, suggesting that ATP levels are glycolysis-dependent in MyPs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1G–H), consistent with previous reports that the aerobic glycolytic enzyme M2 pyruvate kinase isoform (PKM2) is required for progenitor cell function (Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by GO-ATeam2 ATP measurement data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1G-H and citation to previous research.

claim: After inhibiting glycolysis using 2-deoxy-D-glucose (2-DG) with other mitochondrial substrates, 5-FU-treated HSCs showed more rapid decreases in ATP concentration than PBS-treated HSCs.
source: After inhibiting glycolysis using 2-deoxy-D-glucose (2-DG) with other mitochondrial substrates, 5-FU-treated HSCs showed more rapid decreases in ATP concentration than PBS-treated HSCs (Figure 4B–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by GO-ATeam2 ATP measurement data shown in Figure 4B-C.

claim: OXPHOS inhibition by oligomycin without glucose or mitochondrial substrates decreased the ATP concentration to a similar extent in both 5-FU- and PBS-treated HSCs, although 5-FU-treated HSCs showed earlier ATP exhaustion.
source: In contrast, OXPHOS inhibition by oligomycin without glucose or mitochondrial substrates decreased the ATP concentration to a similar extent in both 5-FU- and PBS-treated HSCs, although 5-FU-treated HSCs showed earlier ATP exhaustion (Figure 4D–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by GO-ATeam2 ATP measurement data shown in Figure 4D-E.

claim: 5-FU-treated-HSCs upregulated ATP production via glycolysis, rather than relying on mitochondria.
source: These data suggest that 5-FU-treated-HSCs upregulated ATP production via glycolysis, rather than relying on mitochondria.
evidence: The claim is inferred from ATP measurement data under different metabolic inhibition conditions.

claim: No metabolic changes in glycolysis or OXPHOS were observed in HSCs without cell cycle progression after 5-FU administration (very early phase: day 3; late phase: day 15).
source: Importantly, no metabolic changes in glycolysis or OXPHOS were observed in HSCs without cell cycle progression after 5-FU administration (very early phase: day 3; late phase: day 15) (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–H).
evidence: The claim is supported by GO-ATeam2 ATP measurement data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A-H.

claim: PFKFB3 is the most highly expressed PFKFB isozyme in HSCs.
source: Among the four isozymes of mammalian PFKFB, PFKFB3 is the most favorable for PFK activation (Yalcin et al., 2009), and is the most highly expressed in HSCs (Figure 4F).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: When treated with the PFKFB3-specific inhibitor AZ PFKFB3 26, compared with HSCs from PBS-treated mice, HSCs from 5-FU-treated mice showed decreased ATP levels.
source: When treated with the PFKFB3-specific inhibitor AZ PFKFB3 26 (Boyd et al., 2015), compared with HSCs from PBS-treated mice, HSCs from 5-FU-treated mice showed decreased ATP levels (Figure 4G, I; Figure 4—figure supplement 2I).
evidence: The claim is supported by GO-ATeam2 ATP measurement data shown in Figure 4G, I.

claim: AMPK inhibition by dorsomorphin did not alter ATP concentration in 5-FU-treated-HSCs.
source: Although AMPK activates PFKFB3 in other contexts (Marsin et al., 2002), AMPK inhibition by dorsomorphin did not alter ATP concentration in 5-FU-treated-HSCs (Figure 4H and J).
evidence: The claim is supported by GO-ATeam2 ATP measurement data shown in Figure 4H and J.

claim: Exposure of PBS- or 5-FU-treated HSCs to either etomoxir, a FAO inhibitor, or 6-diazo-5-oxo-L-norleucine (DON), a glutaminolysis inhibitor, alone or in combination, did not decrease ATP concentrations.
source: Exposure of PBS- or 5-FU-treated HSCs to either etomoxir, a FAO inhibitor, or 6-diazo-5-oxo-L-norleucine (DON), a glutaminolysis inhibitor, alone or in combination, did not decrease ATP concentrations (Figure 4—figure supplement 2J–M).
evidence: The claim is supported by GO-ATeam2 ATP measurement data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2J-M.

claim: Neither FAO nor glutaminolysis appeared to be essential for the short-term maintenance of ATP levels in cell-cycling HSCs after 5-FU administration.
source: Thus, neither FAO nor glutaminolysis appeared to be essential for the short-term maintenance of ATP levels in cell-cycling HSCs after 5-FU administration.
evidence: The claim is inferred from ATP measurement data with FAO and glutaminolysis inhibitors.

claim: The addition of glucose and a PFKFB3 inhibitor to etomoxir rapidly reduced ATP concentrations in HSCs.
source: Notably, the addition of glucose and a PFKFB3 inhibitor to etomoxir rapidly reduced ATP concentrations in HSCs (Figure 4—figure supplement 2O–P).
evidence: The claim is supported by GO-ATeam2 ATP measurement data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2O-P.

claim: Etomoxir may partially mimic the effects of oligomycin, indicating that OXPHOS is primarily driven by FAO, but can be compensated by PFKFB3-accelerated glycolysis in HSCs.
source: This suggests that etomoxir may partially mimic the effects of oligomycin, indicating that OXPHOS is primarily driven by FAO, but can be compensated by PFKFB3-accelerated glycolysis in HSCs.
evidence: The claim is inferred from ATP measurement data with etomoxir and PFKFB3 inhibitor.

claim: Exposure of HSCs to DON in combination with a PFKFB3 inhibitor did not decrease ATP concentrations, suggesting that ATP production via glutaminolysis is limited in HSCs.
source: Conversely, exposure of HSCs to DON in combination with a PFKFB3 inhibitor did not decrease ATP concentrations (Figure 4—figure supplement 2O–P), suggesting that ATP production via glutaminolysis is limited in HSCs.
evidence: The claim is supported by GO-ATeam2 ATP measurement data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2O-P and inference from the data.

claim: Oligomycin treatment rapidly depleted ATP in HSCs and all HPC fractions.
source: Oligomycin treatment rapidly depleted ATP in HSCs and all HPC fractions (green lines in Figure 5B–C; Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by GO-ATeam2 ATP measurement data shown in Figure 5B-C.

claim: Treatment with 2-DG decreased ATP concentrations for a short amount of time (~12 min) in HSCs and HPCs, but ATP reduction was less evident than that induced by oligomycin.
source: Treatment with 2-DG decreased ATP concentrations for a short amount of time (~12 min) in HSCs and HPCs, but ATP reduction was less evident than that induced by oligomycin (blue lines in Figure 5B–C; Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by GO-ATeam2 ATP measurement data shown in Figure 5B-C.

claim: The ATP reduction induced by 2-DG treatment was particularly low (~15%) in HSCs, multipotent progenitor cells (MPPs), and common lymphoid progenitors (CLPs) relative to that in common myeloid progenitors (CMPs), granulocytes-macrophage progenitors (GMPs), and megakaryocyte-erythrocyte progenitors (MEPs).
source: The ATP reduction induced by 2-DG treatment was particularly low (~15%) in HSCs, multipotent progenitor cells (MPPs), and common lymphoid progenitors (CLPs) relative to that in common myeloid progenitors (CMPs), granulocytes-macrophage progenitors (GMPs), and megakaryocyte-erythrocyte progenitors (MEPs; Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by GO-ATeam2 ATP measurement data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: ATP concentration remained more stable in HSCs treated with oligomycin and glucose than in those treated only with oligomycin.
source: ATP concentration remained more stable in HSCs treated with oligomycin and glucose than in those treated only with oligomycin. Similar results were not seen in HPCs, indicating that HSCs have the plasticity to upregulate glycolytic ATP production to meet demands (orange lines in Figure 5B–C; Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–D, summarized in Figure 5E).
evidence: The claim is supported by GO-ATeam2 ATP measurement data shown in Figure 5B-C, E.

claim: HSCs have the plasticity to upregulate glycolytic ATP production to meet demands.
source: ATP concentration remained more stable in HSCs treated with oligomycin and glucose than in those treated only with oligomycin. Similar results were not seen in HPCs, indicating that HSCs have the plasticity to upregulate glycolytic ATP production to meet demands (orange lines in Figure 5B–C; Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–D, summarized in Figure 5E).
evidence: The claim is inferred from GO-ATeam2 ATP measurement data comparing HSCs and HPCs.

claim: Rotenone (complex I inhibitor) and carbonyl cyanide 4-(trifluoromethoxy)phenylhydrazone (FCCP, mitochondrial uncoupler) treatments, which inhibit OXPHOS-derived ATP production, also decreased ATP concentrations in HSCs, but not when administered simultaneously with glucose.
source: Similar to oligomycin treatment, rotenone (complex I inhibitor) and carbonyl cyanide 4-(trifluoromethoxy)phenylhydrazone (FCCP, mitochondrial uncoupler) treatments, which inhibit OXPHOS-derived ATP production, also decreased ATP concentrations in HSCs, but not when administered simultaneously with glucose (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by GO-ATeam2 ATP measurement data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E-F.

claim: With oligomycin, HSCs, but not HPCs, maintained ATP concentrations at low glucose levels (50 mg/dL).
source: Furthermore, with oligomycin, HSCs, but not HPCs, maintained ATP concentrations at low glucose levels (50 mg/dL) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: The claim is supported by GO-ATeam2 ATP measurement data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1G.

claim: ATP was produced by mitochondrial OXPHOS in steady-state HSCs, and only HSCs, but not HPCs, maintained ATP production by glycolysis when OXPHOS was compromised.
source: These analyses suggest that ATP was produced by mitochondrial OXPHOS in steady-state HSCs, and that only HSCs, but not HPCs, maintained ATP production by glycolysis when OXPHOS was compromised.
evidence: The claim is inferred from multiple ATP measurement experiments comparing HSCs and HPCs under different conditions.

claim: In oligomycin-treated HSCs, PFKFB3 inhibition led to rapidly decreased ATP concentration that was not observed in HSCs not treated with oligomycin.
source: In oligomycin-treated HSCs, PFKFB3 inhibition led to rapidly decreased ATP concentration that was not observed in HSCs not treated with oligomycin (Figure 5F–I).
evidence: The claim is supported by GO-ATeam2 ATP measurement data shown in Figure 5F-I.

claim: Inhibiting PKM2, which accelerates glycolysis in steady-state progenitors, significantly reduced ATP levels in oligomycin-treated HSCs.
source: Inhibiting PKM2, which accelerates glycolysis in steady-state progenitors (Wang et al., 2014), significantly reduced ATP levels in oligomycin-treated HSCs (Figure 5—figure supplement 1H, J).
evidence: The claim is supported by GO-ATeam2 ATP measurement data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1H, J.

claim: Inhibiting LKB1, a kinase upstream of AMPK, did not affect the ATP concentration in oligomycin-treated HSCs.
source: Inhibiting LKB1, a kinase upstream of AMPK (Hardie, 2014; Long and Zierath, 2006), did not affect the ATP concentration in oligomycin-treated HSCs (Figure 5—figure supplement 1I, K), whereas levels of adenosine monophosphate (AMP), which also activates AMPK, increased in oligomycin-treated but not in 5-FU-treated HSCs (Figure 5—figure supplement 1L).
evidence: The claim is supported by GO-ATeam2 ATP measurement data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1I, K.

claim: Levels of adenosine monophosphate (AMP), which also activates AMPK, increased in oligomycin-treated but not in 5-FU-treated HSCs.
source: Inhibiting LKB1, a kinase upstream of AMPK (Hardie, 2014; Long and Zierath, 2006), did not affect the ATP concentration in oligomycin-treated HSCs (Figure 5—figure supplement 1I, K), whereas levels of adenosine monophosphate (AMP), which also activates AMPK, increased in oligomycin-treated but not in 5-FU-treated HSCs (Figure 5—figure supplement 1L).
evidence: The claim is supported by tracer analysis data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1L.

claim: Unlike HSCs, HPCs exhibited PFKFB3-dependent ATP production, even without oligomycin.
source: Unlike HSCs, HPCs exhibited PFKFB3-dependent ATP production, even without oligomycin (Figure 5—figure supplement 1M–Q).
evidence: The claim is supported by GO-ATeam2 ATP measurement data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1M-Q.

claim: ATP production in steady-state HSCs was PFKFB3-independent, and proliferative stimulation or OXPHOS inhibition plastically activated glycolytic ATP production in a PFKFB3-dependent manner to meet ATP demand.
source: Therefore, ATP production in steady-state HSCs was PFKFB3-independent, and proliferative stimulation or OXPHOS inhibition plastically activated glycolytic ATP production in a PFKFB3-dependent manner to meet ATP demand.
evidence: The claim is inferred from multiple ATP measurement experiments under different conditions.

claim: Pfkfb3-overexpressed HSCs increased the proportion of cells in the S/G2/M phase and decreased the number of G0 cells compared to mock-overexpressed HSCs.
source: Pfkfb3-overexpressed HSCs increased the proportion of cells in the S/G2/M phase and decreased the number of G0 cells compared to mock-overexpressed HSCs (Figure 5K).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell cycle analysis data shown in Figure 5K.

claim: Upon 2-DG treatment, Pfkfb3-overexpressing HSCs showed a greater decrease in ATP concentration than mock-transduced HSCs did.
source: Upon 2-DG treatment, Pfkfb3-overexpressing HSCs showed a greater decrease in ATP concentration than mock-transduced HSCs did (Figure 5L; Figure 5—figure supplement 1S).
evidence: The claim is supported by GO-ATeam2 ATP measurement data shown in Figure 5L.

claim: Oligomycin treatment of both mock-transduced and Pfkfb3-overexpressing HSCs decreased ATP concentration to comparable levels.
source: However, oligomycin treatment of both mock-transduced and Pfkfb3-overexpressing HSCs decreased ATP concentration to comparable levels (Figure 5M; Figure 5—figure supplement 1T).
evidence: The claim is supported by GO-ATeam2 ATP measurement data shown in Figure 5M.

claim: Pfkfb3-overexpressing HSCs recovered ATP levels more effectively under low glucose conditions (12.5 mg/dL) than did mock-transduced HSCs.
source: Notably, Pfkfb3-overexpressing HSCs recovered ATP levels more effectively under low glucose conditions (12.5 mg/dL) than did mock-transduced HSCs (Figure 5M; Figure 5—figure supplement 1U).
evidence: The claim is supported by GO-ATeam2 ATP measurement data shown in Figure 5M.

claim: PFKFB3 directly conferred glycolytic dependence onto HSCs by modulating the cell cycle and increasing their ATP-generating capacity via glycolysis under metabolic stress.
source: These data suggest that PFKFB3 directly conferred glycolytic dependence onto HSCs by modulating the cell cycle and increasing their ATP-generating capacity via glycolysis under metabolic stress.
evidence: The claim is inferred from cell cycle and ATP measurement data in Pfkfb3-overexpressing HSCs.

claim: PFKFB3 transcript and protein levels in HSCs remained unchanged during 5-FU-induced cell cycling.
source: PFKFB3 activity is regulated at multiple levels (Shi et al., 2017), and PFKFB3 transcript and protein levels in HSCs remained unchanged during 5-FU-induced cell cycling (Figure 6A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA sequencing and immunocytochemistry data shown in Figure 6A-B.

claim: No change in PFKFB3 phosphorylation was observed in 5-FU-treated-HSCs.
source: Phosphorylation can also regulate PFKFB3 activity (Marsin et al., 2002; Novellasdemunt et al., 2013; Okamura and Sakakibara, 1998); however, we observed no change in PFKFB3 phosphorylation in 5-FU-treated-HSCs (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunocytochemistry data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Upon oligomycin exposure, PFKFB3 was phosphorylated by AMPK in the HSCs.

claim: Under proliferative stress, HSCs uniformly shift from mitochondrial respiration to glycolytic ATP production and PPP activation, which represent hallmarks of cell-cycling mammalian cells.

Under proliferative stress, HSCs uniformly shift from mitochondrial respiration to glycolytic ATP production and PPP activation, which represent hallmarks of cell-cycling mammalian cells (Intlekofer and Finley, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from tracer analysis and 13C-MFA, and citation to established knowledge.

evidence: The claim is supported by real-time ATP measurement data using GO-ATeam2.

claim: HSCs exposed to acute stresses choose to change the efficiency of glucose utilization (accelerated glycolytic ATP production) rather than other energy sources.

evidence: The claim is inferred from experiments showing HSCs maintain ATP through glycolysis under OXPHOS inhibition.
